description: Frozen from completed S4 engine before extraction. Fixed inputs, seeds, actions, timesteps and complete observable state at checkpoints; not regenerated from candidate code.

steps.say: All traffic goes to checkout-v1. new-checkout is at 0%.
new-checkout goes to 10%: one request in ten lands on v2. It looks fine.
Ramped to 50%.
At volume v2's bug appears: about a third of its requests fail (red). Half of all users are on v2.
Kill switch: rollout to 0. The next request goes to v1 and errors stop.

~14 req/s offered; the gateway admits 12 and sheds the rest as 429s (red). Reads mostly hit Redis.
Traffic nearly doubles. The gateway holds the line at 12 req/s: more 429s, but the APIs and Postgres see the same load and p99 doesn't move.
api-a dies. For 0.6 s the NLB keeps sending to it (refused, red), until its health check notices and api-b takes everything.
api-a is back in rotation.

DNS splits ~600 req/s across both regions. Every write in us-east also crosses to us-west's replica.
us-east's load balancer goes dark. Clients still hold DNS answers pointing at it: their requests are refused (red).
The TTL has run out; DNS answers only with us-west, which now carries everything.
us-east is back and DNS returns it to the rotation.

INSERT creates a row. Reusing an existing key is a conflict.
The write commits, but its reply exceeds the timeout. The retry reuses the same key and conflicts.
Follow a request: a timeout does not mean that its write was rolled back.
UPSERT preserves one row per key. Repeated writes still create versions; the timeout remains.
Latency recovers. Upserts now succeed without retries; conflicts have stopped.

Every write waits for all in-sync replicas. Partition 0 takes half the traffic, so ledger-a (which owns it) works hardest.
Broker 0 dies. Partition 0 loses its leader and pauses for an election (dim lane); writes to it fail and are retried.
A new leader is elected. With 2 of 3 replicas in sync, min ISR is still met: writes flow again.
Broker 1 dies too. Every partition is down to 1 in-sync replica, under min ISR 2: with acks=all every write is refused.
Both brokers return and rejoin the ISR; writes resume and the consumers catch up.

Shorter transactions drain the waiters. Locks remain enabled and lost updates stay at zero.

Orders flow in at ~400/s. Billing and the search indexer read orders.v1 as separate consumer groups; both keep up.
billing-a crashes. The billing group pauses to rebalance, then billing-b owns all three partitions: 8 rec/s against ~10 coming in.
Billing lag climbs (bright cells, the white cursor falls behind). Search is unaffected: its blue cursor stays at the head.
billing-a returns, the group rebalances again and the backlog drains.

The CDN answers 60% of requests; the rest reach the API, which reads through Redis (85% hit) and publishes every order to Kafka and a job to the queue.
Redis dies. Its calls are refused, so those requests fail; reads that missed still reach Postgres.
Redis is back. Now a billing consumer dies: the group rebalances and billing lag climbs.
Both consumers are back and the backlog drains.

Each PUT /profile writes to the primary, then reads the profile back from the replica to return it. The replica applies the WAL almost at once, though concurrent writes can still race reads.
The replica starts applying the WAL 4 s late (amber: rows behind the primary). The read-back often gets the previous version.
Follow one request: the upsert writes a new version to the primary; the read-back from the replica returns an older version or a missing row, marked stale.
The fix: read your own write from the primary. The replica is still behind, but nobody reads it straight after writing.
The replica catches up.

~180 req/s. inventory answers in ~25 ms, well inside orders-api's 150 ms timeout.
inventory slows to ~260 ms (a bad query plan). Calls start timing out; each one is retried up to 3 times (amber).
The storm: inventory now sees several times the real traffic, its buffer fills (amber cells) and it answers 503. Almost nothing succeeds.
A breaker on the call. It trips open (red port): calls fail fast without touching inventory, so its load collapses.
inventory is fixed. The breaker half-opens (amber), its trial call succeeds, and it closes.
